title: OOM resilience ladder and localized fallback playbook (draft)
summary: Working draft for a staged mitigation ladder and localized fallback strategy when a serving-runtime host or tenant experiences rapid memory traction leading to OOMs or eviction cascades. Includes playbook steps, quick triage commands, metrics to watch, and follow-ups for engineering.
incident_context: We observed several short-lived OOM spikes over the last month where tenant-local KV cache growth + sustained continuous-batching load caused host memory pressure, followed by eviction storms that pushed other tenants into micro-OOMs and increased tail latency. This doc explores a pragmatic oncall ladder that prioritizes containment, graceful degradation, and fast recovery while minimizing cross-tenant blast radius.
impact_observed:
- Increased 99th token latency from 120ms -> 650ms for affected hosts
- 4 hosts entered OOM kill in a 7 minute window
- Upstream request queuing increased, causing client-side retries and higher request concurrency
- ~3% error rate bump for affected customer routes
- KV eviction count spiked and persisted for ~30m after the initial OOMs
high_level_goals: 1) Contain memory pressure to as small a set of hosts/tenants as possible. 2) Provide graceful fallback for latency-sensitive routes. 3) Stabilize KV cache growth and prevent repeated host restarts. 4) Collect telemetry and evidentiary artifacts for post-incident RCA.
primary_hypotheses:
- KV cache async-prefetch combined with a large prefix cache for a small number of tenants caused latent memory amplification.
- Continuous-batching scheduler held large microbatches open when host CPU throttled, increasing resident set size.
- A rare allocation path in quantized kernels leaks transient buffers under high concurrency.
- Eviction-throttle misconfiguration caused slow reclaim and cascading evictions.
quick_triage_commands:
1) Check host health and OOM logs: kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> -c serving-runtime --tail=1000 | egrep -i 'oom|kill|oom_kill'
2) Recent memory metrics: kubectl top pod <pod> --containers; or look at grafana panel 'host_mem_rss_bytes'
3) KV cache evictions: curl -s http://<pod>:8080/metrics | grep redwood_kv_cache_evictions_total
4) Batching queue length: curl -s http://<pod>:8080/internal/queue | jq .queue_lengths
5) Identify tenants allocating most memory: /admin/tenant-metrics endpoint or query perfstore: SELECT tenant_id, rss_peak FROM host_rss_samples WHERE host='<host>' ORDER BY rss_peak DESC LIMIT 10
containment_ladder:
Level 0 - immediate shorthand: mark host as maintenance to stop new LB traffic and let in-flight requests drain.
Level 1 - per-tenant pinning: move top-3 offending tenants to safe-mode (pin to smaller cache config) using dynconfig (PATCH /dynconfig/tenants/<tenant>/cache -> low-water).
Level 2 - localized eviction aggressor rule: set eviction multiplier to 2x only for affected host via dynconfig host label.
Level 3 - fallback routing: route latency-critical routes to warm fallback model variant (lower KV footprint) via routing policy.
Level 4 - host reboot: if repeated OOMs or unresponsive, cordon + drain + recycle host. Only after containment steps attempted.
mitigation_commands:
- mark host unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl annotate pod <pod> redwood/scheduled-for-maintenance=true
- reduce tenant cache window: curl -X PATCH -d '{"cache_window_sec":60}' https://dynconfig.internal/tenants/<tenant>
- flip batching fallback: curl -X POST https://runtime.internal/flags -d '{"continuous_batching": "fallback"}' (use only during emergency)
- trigger immediate GC/flush: POST /admin/kv/flush?force=true for tenant-specific shards (be conservative)
- increase eviction aggressiveness: curl -X PATCH https://dynconfig.internal/hosts/<host_id> -d '{"eviction_factor":2.0}'
monitoring_checks: OOM kills count increment on host within 10m
post_incident_actions:
- Collect heap profs from last 3 crashes and upload to /artifacts/oom-profiles/<timestamp>
- Create an investigation ticket (RED-XXXX) to reproduce under load and tighten guardrails
- Add per-tenant cache residency quota experiments to Dedicated to prevent single-tenant storms
- Schedule a runbook review and tabletop with oncall rotation
- Instrument an automatic short-circuit: if host_kv_eviction_rate > threshold, automatically reduce batching window for 10m
runbook_steps:
1) Announce on #sre-oncall with short summary and affected hosts/tenants.
2) Run quick triage commands (see above) and paste outputs.
3) Execute containment ladder level 1 -> verify metrics after 60s.
4) If still unhealthy, progress to level 2 and notify engineering lead.
5) If queue/backpressure persists move to routing fallback (level 3).
6) If host continues to OOM, cordon and recycle host. Preserve logs/artifacts.
7) Open postmortem stub and tag relevant owners.
8) Execute follow-ups and assign tickets for permanent fixes.

- Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/serving/host-memory-and-batching

- Kibana logs filter: https://kibana.redwood.ai/app/discover#/?q=serving-runtime%20OOM
notes_to_self:
- Avoid global eviction multiplier flips; those have previously caused cross-host regressions.
- When flushing KV for tenant, prefer targeted shard flushes not full-cache wipes.
- The continuous-batching fallback flag is powerful but will increase cost and latency; annotate any toggle with reason and duration.
- Need a smoke test that recreates eviction storm locally (idea: synthetic tenant that prefetches many long prefixes while sending frequent small requests).
followup_ideas:
- Implement per-tenant memory quotas and eviction isolation.
- Add an automated playbook run that executes level-1 steps when host_rss crosses X for Y minutes.
- Instrument a 'cache pressure' signal emitted from prefetchers to the scheduler to avoid holding microbatches open when memory pressure is rising.
- Add more granular telemetry around per-tenant transient allocations inside quantized kernels.
final_reminder:
This is a working sketch. Test all mitigation steps in staging before applying in prod. Keep the oncall flow as short as possible and prioritize containment over perfection.
